title: malloc and allocated storage
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C rules.
Trace the example and identify data or resource flow.
Recognize relevant safety and failure cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: malloc requests a block of allocated storage of the specified number of bytes and returns a pointer suitably aligned for objects with fundamental alignment requirements. The contents are indeterminate. If allocation fails, malloc returns a null pointer.
understand.whyItMatters: Dynamic allocation supports data whose size is decided at runtime, but every allocation must be checked and its size calculation must be correct.
understand.analogy: Treat each object or stream as a resource with a defined lifetime and explicit rules for access.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal object, storage-duration, alignment or library rules.

explain.narrative:
malloc requests a block of allocated storage of the specified number of bytes and returns a pointer suitably aligned for objects with fundamental alignment requirements. The contents are indeterminate. If allocation fails, malloc returns a null pointer.

Check all allocation, I/O and conversion results. Respect object bounds and lifetime, initialize data before reading it, and define who owns and releases each resource.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The program allocates enough bytes for five int objects, checks for failure, initializes each element before reading it and frees the allocation exactly once.

practise.guidedTask: Calculate the requested allocation size for five and fifty int values.
practise.independentTask: Allocate an array based on a validated runtime count. Explain how the program handles zero and excessive counts.
hints: Use sizeof *pointer to keep allocation size consistent with the pointed-to type.
malloc does not initialize the allocated bytes.
Check count multiplication for overflow before allocating when count can be untrusted.
